answer_text:
Let  
\[
a=1978.
\]
“Last three digits are equal” means
\[
a^n\equiv a^m \pmod{1000}.
\]
Since \(1000=8\cdot 125\), check modulo \(8\) and modulo \(125\).

### Modulo \(8\)

\[
1978\equiv 2 \pmod 8.
\]
The powers of \(2\) modulo \(8\) are
\[
2^1\equiv 2,\qquad 2^2\equiv 4,\qquad 2^e\equiv 0\quad(e\ge 3)\pmod 8.
\]
Since \(n>m\ge 1\), if \(m=1\) or \(m=2\), then \(a^n\) cannot match \(a^m\) modulo \(8\). Therefore any solution must have
\[
m\ge 3,
\]
and then both \(a^m\) and \(a^n\) are \(0\pmod 8\).

### Modulo \(125\)

\[
1978\equiv 103 \pmod{125},
\]
and \(\gcd(103,125)=1\). Thus
\[
1978^n\equiv 1978^m \pmod{125}
\]
is equivalent to
\[
103^{n-m}\equiv 1 \pmod{125}.
\]
So \(n-m\) must be a multiple of the order of \(103\) modulo \(125\).

Compute that order:
\[
103^2\equiv 109 \pmod{125},
\]
\[
103^4\equiv 109^2\equiv 6 \pmod{125},
\]
\[
103^5\equiv 6\cdot 103\equiv 118 \pmod{125},
\]
\[
103^{10}\equiv 118^2\equiv 49 \pmod{125},
\]
\[
103^{20}\equiv 49^2\equiv 26 \pmod{125},
\]
\[
103^{25}\equiv 103^{20}\cdot 103^5\equiv 26\cdot 118\equiv 68 \pmod{125},
\]
\[
103^{50}\equiv 68^2\equiv 4624\equiv 124\equiv -1 \pmod{125}.
\]
Hence
\[
103^{100}\equiv 1 \pmod{125}.
\]
The order divides \(\varphi(125)=100\). The computations above rule out all proper divisors of \(100\), so the order is exactly
\[
100.
\]

Therefore
\[
n-m\ge 100.
\]
Also \(m\ge 3\), so
\[
m+n=2m+(n-m)\ge 2\cdot 3+100=106.
\]

This minimum is achieved by taking
\[
m=3,\qquad n=3+100=103.
\]
Indeed, modulo \(8\) both powers are \(0\), and modulo \(125\),
\[
1978^{103}\equiv 1978^3\cdot 1978^{100}\equiv 1978^3\pmod{125},
\]
so the last three digits match modulo \(1000\).

Thus the minimizing pair is

\[
\boxed{(m,n)=(3,103)\text{ and }m+n_{\min}=106}
\]
